item.title: DoD pushes out 3 loans totaling $450M to bolster US space companies
item.dc:creator: Theresa Hitchens
item.description: One industry source told Breaking Defense that the reason for the spate of new loan announcements is that the Pentagon “needed to finalize loans by the end of the fiscal year.”
item.content:encoded:
WASHINGTON ― The Defense Department’s Office of Strategic Capital has recently announced three loans, worth a total of $450 million, to US space firms to bolster launch and space monitoring capacities.

The most recent of these was a $150 million loan to Rocket Lab, announced on Monday, to help the firm “increase the flight rate of its reusable Neutron rocket beyond first launch to meet growing commercial and national security demand for access to space.”

Rocket Lab last month confirmed that Neutron’s first launch has been delayed from late this year until sometime next year. The firm originally had planned to launch the medium-lift rocket in 2024, then pushed that date back to late 2025.

Another $150 million loan was awarded on Oct. 26 to startup Stoke Space to help it build a second launch pad at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida for its planned Nova reusable rocket. Stoke originally had hoped to launch Nova in 2025, but now is planning lift off in March 2027.

Those two awards attest to the Pentagon’s growing unease about a potential gap in the availability of space launch vehicles post 2028, when SpaceX will stop flying commercial payloads on Falcon 9. An Oct. 29 report by Quilty Space found a likely shortfall of at least 150 launches between now and 2030, including for military payloads as Space Force demand increases.

Both Rocket Lab and Stoke were added in March 2025 to the Space Force’s pool of potential launch providers under the service’s National Security Space Launch (NSSL) Phase 3 Lane 1 program, which covers launches to easier to reach orbits, payloads with less mass, and missions that are not absolute must-goes.

The Pentagon also announced on Nov. 4 a loan worth $150 million to space monitoring firm LeoLabs to “accelerate the deployment of critical radar infrastructure and advanced decision science software,” in particular, deployment of the company’s new Scout mobile radar.

According to a Nov. 5 LeoLabs announcement, the award will help expand its domestic radar manufacturing capacity, including completion of “two large-scale manufacturing facilities by 2028.”

One industry source told Breaking Defense that the reason for the spate of new loan announcements is that the Pentagon “needed to finalize loans by the end of the fiscal year” and thus “have been rolling them out on a regular cadence since.” (While fiscal 2026 officially ended Sept. 30, DoD contract announcements often don’t come until after actual awards to allow for official paperwork to be completed.)

This spate of year-end activity by the Office of Strategic Capital includes loans for non-space related activities as well.

For example, DoD on Nov. 2 announced a “loan commitment of up to $450 million” to startup drone maker Neros to support the firm’s “planned expansion of vertically integrated domestic manufacturing capacity” to produce dual-use sUAS [small unmanned aircraft systems] platforms, ground control systems, and critical components like motors, radios, flight electronics, sensors, and batteries.”

And on Nov. 5, a $75 million loan to Halo Industries was announced to help the California-based firm scale production of its “innovative Silicon Carbide (SiC) semiconductor wafers.”

Like all loans granted by the Office of Strategic Capital, the three space company loans are “conditional,” requiring a process of due diligence about the grantee’s finances. In addition, the loans require a matching investment of company capital.

The office was created by DoD in 2022 under the Office of the Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering, and subsequently was authorized by Congress to run a pilot investment program in the FY24 National Defense Authorization Act to run through FY28.

According to a September report by the Congressional Research Service, the Office of Strategic Capital’s remit includes both “direct debt financing for companies and the financing of venture capital, private equity, and other investment funds,” as well as “loans and loan guarantees to third-party investment funds.”

Further, the report explained that for FY26, Congress appropriated $97.8 million for its “capital assistance pilot program,” designed to “subsidize up to $4.4 billion in loans, loan guarantees, and technical assistance.” The Office of Strategic Capital also received $2 million for FY26 through the defense-wide research, development, test, and evaluation (RDT&E) account.

The office put out its first notice of $984 million in direct loan funding availability on a “rolling basis” in September 2024, accompanied by a Federal Register notice that listed 34 categories of dual-use technology for potential investment. While the office is focused largely on microelectronics and computer-related tech, three of these are space specific: “space launch; spacecraft; and space-enabled services and equipment.” Several more are space adjacent, including optical communications, sensor hardware and solar power.

The September CRS report added that the Pentagon’s FY27 budget request said the office would use $20 million in FY25 reconciliation funding for RDT&E activities during in FY26.

The FY27 request further includes $216 million in discretionary funding and $20 billion in mandatory funding for the Office of Strategic Capital’s capital assistance pilot program, as well as $19 million for the office’s RDT&E activities, CRS found.

item.title: Poland says Pentagon supports permanent US base, with decision expected in December
item.dc:creator: Bartosz Głowacki
item.description: Warsaw has identified four potential locations for a base that could accommodate 5,000 US troops and their families, and is offering to spend up to $4.4 billion on supporting infrastructure.
item.content:encoded:
WARSAW — A White House decision on establishing a permanent US military base in Poland could come as early as next month, the country’s defense minister said following discussions with US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth at the Pentagon.

In a statement released after Tuesday’s meeting, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defence Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said Hegseth indicated “everything is going in a good direction” when asked about the status of the proposal. Kosiniak-Kamysz characterized the response as a “green light” from the Pentagon for a permanent US troop presence, while acknowledging that the final decision rests with the White House.

That decision is expected in early December, he said.

“The permanent presence of US troops in Poland is our absolute priority and we will not abandon this matter,” Kosiniak-Kamysz said.

“This is likely my most important and ground-breaking visit to the US,” he added. “I can confidently say that Poland is not only a model ally of the United States, but [has also become] its strategic partner.”

A Pentagon readout of the Tuesday meeting said Hegseth recognized Poland’s leadership in NATO as European allies assume greater responsibility for their conventional defense. The two officials also signed a Statement of Intent to strengthen bilateral defense industrial cooperation, building on Poland’s increased defense spending and expanding role in the US industrial base.

“Whether it’s committing to nearly 5 percent of [gross domestic product] to defense and translating that investment into ready forces and sustained combat power, Poland is building one of the most formidable armies in Europe, ready to secure and defend its territory,” Hegseth said in a statement.

The Defense Department did not respond to Breaking Defense’s request for comment by the time of publication.

Warsaw has identified four potential locations for the base: Bydgoszcz, Poznań, Szczecin and Wrocław. The cities are all west of the Vistula River, which Kosiniak-Kamysz said aligns with US preferences.

Each location already has Polish, US or NATO military infrastructure, including NATO command facilities in Bydgoszcz and Szczecin and the US Army’s forward headquarters in Poznań. Wrocław is located near major military training grounds at Żagań and Świętoszów and has access to the A4 motorway and airport infrastructure designed to support military airlift operations.

The proposed installation would need to accommodate as many as 25,000 people, including approximately 5,000 US troops, their families and accompanying support personnel, Kosiniak-Kamysz told Polish newspaper Rzeczpospolita on Tuesday. Poland has offered to cover the infrastructure costs, which Kosiniak-Kamysz estimated in September at between 15 billion and 17 billion zlotys ($3.8 billion to $4.4 billion).

“We are ready. We have prepared the sites, and we are prepared to construct the necessary infrastructure and secure the required funding,” Kosiniak-Kamysz said.

Kosiniak-Kamysz has argued that a permanent US presence would strengthen Poland’s security and position on NATO’s eastern flank, while also allowing Polish forces to assume a greater share of responsibility for regional security.

The discussions come as the Trump administration pushes for a rebalancing of NATO under its “NATO 3.0” concept, which envisions European allies taking primary responsibility for the continent’s conventional defense while the US shifts focus to other regions.

Kosiniak-Kamysz has previously said the shift could involve deeper transatlantic defense industrial cooperation. In October, he called for US companies to relocate production lines and maintenance facilities to Europe — including for Patriot missile systems — and pursue joint ventures with European manufacturers.

Tuesday’s discussions also touched on Poland’s request to purchase Tomahawk cruise missiles and associated launchers, Kosiniak-Kamysz told reporters after the meeting. After submitting the request “several months ago,” he said the Pentagon had issued a “positive recommendation” on the proposed sale, but that the final decision rests with Congress.

Further, the US Defense Department announced in October that Poland had been selected to host the first Patriot PAC-3 missile maintenance facility outside the United States, a move intended to strengthen missile sustainment capabilities in Europe and deepen bilateral defense industrial cooperation.

Speaking on Monday at the Transatlantic Defense Industry Access Forum in Warsaw, Polish Secretary of State in the Ministry of National Defence Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka said it was time for the countries’ longstanding defense industrial relationship to expand.

“I think that the decision from two weeks ago to place the first Patriot PAC-3 missiles service center in the world outside the US on Polish territory is terrific evidence of a new chapter in the trade relationship between the United States and Poland,” Sobkowiak-Czarnecka said.

Ashley Roque contributed to this report.

item.title: EU sets out $3.4B defense budget for 2027, boosts Ukraine spending
item.dc:creator: Tim Martin
item.description: The new fiscal uplift comes in the wake of Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy telling European leaders last month that “we need at least €70 billion more from you.”
item.content:encoded:
BELFAST — The European Parliament and the Council of the European Union have agreed to a 2027 defense and security budget valued at €3.1 ($3.4 billion), the bloc announced, spurred by the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East.

“To step up to the challenge of the current geopolitical situation” next year’s annual budget includes “major support to Ukraine,” based on Ukraine Support Loan funding and the Ukraine Facility, according to an EU statement released today.

The Ukraine Support Loan funding for the year is listed at €650 million, a boost to the previously promised pool of €90 billion. (The Ukraine Facility is a separate mechanism designed to facilitates tens of billions of euros to Kyiv in grants and loans.)

The announcement comes a month after Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told European leaders that “we need at least €70 billion more from you” on top of the promised €90 billion in loans as the war with Russia looks set to enter its fifth year.

The UK’s Guardian newspaper reported that the EU appears to have heard Zelenskyy’s call, promising to dig up €45 billion with the remaining shortfall potentially made up by Canada and the UK. It wasn’t immediately clear how the recently announced budget plays into the proposed €45 billion, and a spokesperson for the bloc did not respond to a request for comment today.

The 2027 budget is the last from the EU’s existing Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), before members decide on a new version covering longer-term spending plans between 2028-2034.

Those discussions are reportedly already engulfed in geopolitical drama. The Financial Times reported that German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has warned that he will block the future, multiyear budget, should any EU member states refuse to provide financial support for Ukraine. Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic previously opted out of the EU’s initial €90 billion loan. Those three nations and Bulgaria have also signaled that they won’t contribute to future lending.

“A collective commitment that all of us, without exception, will contribute fairly to closing [Ukraine’s financing] gap is an essential prerequisite for resolving this issue and for discussing any further matters, particularly those with financial implications,” Merz purportedly wrote in a letter sent to European Council President António Costa, per the business news outlet.
 
Outside of how future budget negotiations play out, the EU’s own budget preparation documents make clear that maintaining monetary support for the war-torn nation, while in parallel reacting to other regional or international events has become an increasingly difficult task. 

“The EU budget has shown versatility, but it also demonstrated the limits of its current architecture, thus requiring a mid-term revision to adequately address additional needs for Ukraine, migration and its root causes, responding to the crises in the Middle East, reinforcing our capacity to respond to natural disasters, and support for boosting investments in critical technologies and defence,” noted a European Commission statement of estimates for FY2027.
